div.head: Duns 1
div.ab: Ðæt is: gif man trode bedrifð forstolenes yrfes of stæðe on oðer, ðonne befæste man þæt spo[r] landesmannum oððe mid mearce gecyðe, þæt man riht drife.
Hoc est: si uestigium furati pecoris minetur de loco in locum, tunc committatur ipsum uestigium landhominibus uel cum marca monstretur, quod rectum prosequantur.

Nämlich: (Von der Spur gestohlenen Viehes. lq) Wenn jemand die Fährte gestohlenen Viehes von einem [Wye-?]Ufer ans andere leitet, dann übergebe er diesen Spurfaden [dort] heimischen Leuten, beziehungsweise [falls er ihn jenseits verlor] erweise durch Merkmal, dass er Rechtliches verfolge.

Namely: (Of the track of stolen cattle. lq) If anyone follows the track of stolen cattle from one [Wye?] bank to the other, then let him hand over that trail to the people of the land [there], or [if he lost it on the far side] show by a mark that he is pursuing [it] lawfully.

That is, if a man follows up the track of stolen cattle from one bank to the other [across the river], then he [shall] entrust that trail to the local people or prove with evidence that he is making a legal pursuit.
div.note: U: translator unrecorded: check; B reads ‘spon’; Liebermann supplies ‘spor’ from Ld. The rubrics marked ‘lq’ come from the lost exemplar of Ld and the Quadripartitus and are not original. Liebermann compares VI As 8.4.

Q verwechselt (auch 1, 2. 2. 6) das Wort mit stede, wie er denn 2, 2 dafür steðe unübersetzt lässt.—Dass die Grenze stream, was ‘Strom’ wie ‘Bach’ und ‘Wassergraben’ bedeuten kann, bildet, sagt c. 8. Vgl. Archiv S. 292f. Dass ein Fluss Grenzscheide zwischen Stämmen bildet, ist der Engl. Siedlung eigen; Leeds Archaeol. of Agsax. settlem. 22

Q confuses the word (also at 1, 2. 2. 6) with stede, just as at 2, 2 he leaves steðe untranslated in its place.—That the boundary is formed by the stream, which can mean ‘river’ as well as ‘brook’ and ‘ditch’, is stated in c. 8. Cf. Archiv p. 292f. That a river forms the dividing line between peoples is characteristic of English settlement; Leeds Archaeol. of Agsax. settlem. 22

‘und’ ändert Thorpe (auch Earle) ohne Grund. Das ‘oder’ bedeutet nicht etwa des Klägers Wahl, ob er die Einheimischen anrufen oder selbst die jenseitige Spur weiter verfolgen wolle. Letzteres widerspräche c. 6

Thorpe (and also Earle) alters this to ‘and’ without reason. The ‘or’ does not mean, say, that the plaintiff may choose whether to call on the inhabitants or to follow the trail further on the other side himself. The latter would contradict c. 6

Vielleicht versteht Q laut des cum das Wort als ‘Grenze’, was falsche Wahl zwischen den Bedd. [und übtr. deren ‘Bewohnerschaft’ (s. u. 2²; Gl Grenzgericht 1), was fürs Ags. mearc unbelegt] wäre.—Vgl. Gl Merkmal; Beweismittel 4a.—Der Verlierer beweist durch Hausmarke Eigentum auch am Funde; J. Hübner Fund im Germ. Recht 43. 131

Perhaps Q, to judge by the cum, understands the word as ‘boundary’, which would be a wrong choice between the meanings [and, by transference, its ‘inhabitants’ (see below 2²; Gl Grenzgericht 1), which is unattested for A.-S. mearc].—Cf. Gl Merkmal; Beweismittel 4a.—The person who has lost a thing proves ownership by his house-mark even of a found object; J. Hübner Fund im Germ. Recht 43. 131

Not an adverb, as Thorpe and Schmid translate
